blocks.text: How Detrimental will Climate Change be to Society? Let’s put the Question to a Prediction Market

The Super El Niño of 2026-2027 offers a rare opportunity to shed some empirical light on one of the most persistent and consequential controversies in contemporary science and politics: How much harm does climate change do to the global economy?

runs.t: Ever since the societal impacts of human-caused climate change
first began to be considered quantitatively in the 1970s
, controversy has persisted over the
severity
of those impacts.
Many
general-audience
and
academic treatments
have depicted
apocalyptic scenarios
of societal collapse, while others,
myself included
, have contended that economic and technological progress has, and will continue to, allow
adaptation to climate change
that not only ameliorates but, in most cases, outpaces
the negative impacts of warming
The most common metric for measuring climate change's impact on human well-being is
economic production
and, more specifically,
global GDP per capita
. These estimates are often further compressed into a number known as the
Social Cost of Carbon
, which purports to represent the dollar value of lost global economic production from a single additional metric ton of CO2 emissions.
Thus, the controversy over the magnitude of climate change's impact on society is reflected in a
very
wide range of published estimates
of the Social Cost of Carbon that spans multiple orders of magnitude.
Although the range is wide, it has a long tail on the severe end, and
most
studies over the decades have found that the economic impacts of climate change represent a small
drag
on economic
growth
and nothing akin to economic or societal collapse. This state has been described as pitting ‘scientists’ on the more pessimistic side and ‘economists’ on the more optimistic side (e.g.,
PBS: Economists and Scientists Deeply Disagree About the Cost of Climate Change
The optimistic economic results have always frustrated activists in the climate movement. For example, when
William Nordhaus
won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economics for pioneering the field of climate-economics (and
advocating a carbon tax to curb emissions along the way
), the decision was met with
hostility from the climate movement
because Nordhaus’s representation of climate change's economic impact was considered insufficiently severe.
A distillation of the controversy has recently been embodied by a high-profile study by economists Adrien Bilal of Stanford and Diego Känzig of Northwestern
(Bilal and Känzig 2026)
, which opens with:

“Climate change is frequently described as one of the defining economic challenges of our time. This view, however, stands in sharp contrast to empirical estimates of its impact on economic activity: they imply that a permanent 1ºC rise in temperature reduces world output by 1%–3%.”
They go on to say,
“In this article, we show that the macroeconomic effects of climate change are an order of magnitude larger than previously documented.”
And
“Our estimates imply that a permanent 1°C rise in global temperature lowers world GDP by over 20%.”
“Our results point to significant economic costs of climate change. They are comparable to the U.S. Great Depression of 1929, but experienced permanently.”
This research, first published as a preprint,
was
widely
celebrated
by those in the climate movement for finally giving academic weight to their intuition about the existential dangers of climate change. In fact, one of the coauthors themselves, Diego Känzig,
explained the value of the paper as such

“When we read the newspapers and when we listen to the scientists, climate change is always portrayed as this existential threat that poses significant risks to our lives, livelihoods, and also the economy, but then when you look at these previous estimates, it doesn't look too severe so that was a tension and it's why when we arrived at these estimates they aligned better with my priors.”
Subsequent studies (e.g.,
Kahn (2026)
and
Curtin and Burgess (2026)) have challenged
Bilal and Känzig on various technical and conceptual grounds.

This resembles the launch/continuation of a perpetually inconclusive controversy typical of academic disputes where claims are so model-dependent and imbued with assumptions (both in the narrow sense of parameter values and model structure and in the broader sense of the ethical values encoded into the models) that they can persist in tension infinitely because they are practically unfalsifiable.
However, Bilal and Känzig (2026) is a bit different than other climate-economic claims due to the confluence of three attributes:
Bilal and Känzig (2026) is part of a
broader
literature
that
attempts
to
quantify

a general relationship between temperature and economic activity from natural variation in the historical record. This means that if we observe large enough short-term (natural) fluctuations in global average temperature, Bilal and Känzig (2026) predict specific consequences for the economy within time horizons short enough to practically detect and measure.

Bilal and Känzig (2026)’s claimed impact of global temperature variations on economic output is so large that it should be directly detectable in raw global GDP per capita, provided that the causal global temperature fluctuation was large enough.
We are currently in the midst of perhaps the
largest

short-term warming fluctuation in global average temperature in the instrumental record. The past three years have been the warmest on record, and the current super El Niño promises to push global temperatures well beyond those records by the end of 2027.
Thus, the next few years offer a very unique opportunity to adjudicate one of the most important questions in economics and politics: How much does temperature change impact the global economy?
That is why I am introducing a ForecastEx prediction market contract customized to test the claims of Bilal and Känzig (2026).
The contract translates the ongoing spike in global temperature into a prediction for the global GDP per capita over the next several years. Specifically, the event question is:
Will world GDP per capita grow by more than 1.1% a year, on average, from 2026 to 2031?
I expand on the origin of the specific numbers below, including why the cutoff depends on how warm 2027 turns out - and introducing a conditional contract along the way.
A “No” outcome aligns with Bilal and Känzig (2026) and the climate movement's broader concerns.
A “Yes” outcome aligns with conventional climate economics and more sanguine views of climate change's impact on society.
The idea is to
use a prediction market to make a consequential claim more testable while reducing the pull toward any preferred conclusion
and, thus, motivated cognition.
This contract resembles the famous
Simon–Ehrlich wager
in that it forces precise terms and conditions on a debate that is typically dominated by adjectives, and it challenges adversaries to put their money where their mouth is.

If someone takes a strong rhetorical public position in this debate but is unwilling to purchase a contract aligned with it, it may be fair to question their true conviction. At the very least, interrogating the reasons for any party's reluctance to engage should force caveats to the surface, which would be revealing in and of itself.

blocks.text: Methods of Bilal and Känzig (2026) and the derivation of the prediction market contract specifications

runs.t: Global warming is a gradual upward trend of about 0.2°C (0.36°F) per decade, but the planet’s average temperature does not rise smoothly. It climbs in steps, rising or falling from one year to the next by several tenths of a degree or more. The largest single cause of those swings is the El Niño- La Niña cycle.

El Niño is a warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean's surface waters that recurs irregularly, every two to seven years. While it lasts, the ocean releases a large amount of stored heat into the atmosphere, raising the global average surface temperature. The effect lags by several months, so the warmest year usually comes just after an El Niño peaks (orange dots in Figure 1).

caption.t: Global average surface temperature relative to the 1901–2000 average. Orange dots mark years that began during a strong El Niño (a December–February Oceanic Niño Index of at least 1.5 °C). Values for 2026 and 2027 are estimates that are updated monthly. The bars at right mark the three ranges of NOAA’s 2027 value that the conditional contracts are tied to. Data from NOAA, plotted in Python.

runs.t: An El Niño is currently underway, and the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimates a very high chance that it will be the strongest in NOAA’s record, almost guaranteeing 2027 will be the warmest year on record (barring a major volcanic eruption that can work to cool the global climate for a year or more).

blocks.text: The Bilal and Känzig estimate of the impact

runs.t: Bilal and Känzig (2026) estimate how global GDP per capita changes in the years after what they call global temperature “shocks”, which are departures of global temperature from its trend, measured as the gap between a year’s temperature and what the temperatures of two and three years earlier would have predicted.

Their central claim is that a 1°C global temperature shock is followed by world GDP per capita about 12% lower six years later than it would otherwise have been (Figure 2; their country-by-country estimate, which weights every country equally, is 14%). Applied to permanent warming, the estimates imply that each 1°C of warming eventually lowers world output by more than 20%.

caption.t: The paper’s central estimate of how world GDP per person responds to a 1 °C global temperature shock, with its 90% range. Re-estimated from the authors’ replication data, plotted in Python.

runs.t: World economic production is represented by the World Bank’s figure for world GDP per capita, adjusted for inflation and price differences between countries. The contract compares its growth from 2026 to 2031 with what that growth would have been if temperature shocks had no effect. I begin the temperature shock with the record warmth of 2023 and end it at the end of 2027.
To assess the effect of the ongoing temperature shock on global GDP per capita, we need to compare what takes place with what we would expect to have taken place without it.

This means we need to estimate a counterfactual expectation that serves as the null hypothesis. To do so, I try to be as conventional as possible by using the International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projection, converted to growth per person. That projection has world GDP per person growing by 2.4% in 2027, 2.3% in 2028, 2.3% in 2029, 2.2% in 2030, and 2.1% in 2031, an average of 2.26% a year (Figure 3).

Of course, the world economy is not perfectly predictable, and events like the 2009 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic were not predicted years in advance and each knocked several points off a single year’s growth.

I try to build this uncertainty into the baseline estimate by documenting how far off the IMF’s October forecasts of world growth, made every year from 1990 to 2020, were over the following years, including recessions. That record also indicates a sign bias. Over five-year stretches like 2027–2031, world growth came in about 3.1 percentage points below the IMF’s forecast on average (about 0.6 points a year), and it fell short in 27 of the 31 stretches. I thus subtract this IMF tendency to overestimate growth from the experiment period.
What I arrive at is that with no temperature effect at all, average growth from 2026 to 2031 would most likely be about 1.6% a year, landing between 1.0% and 2.3% a year with an 80% likelihood.

caption.t: Yearly growth in world GDP per person, 1991–2025, and the outlook for 2027–2031. Gray: the IMF’s October 2026 projection. Blue: the no-effect baseline, which is that projection less the IMF’s average past miss. The shaded band is the 80% range for average growth over 2026–2031 if temperature shocks have no effect; the dashed orange line is the paper’s estimate. Data from the World Bank and the IMF, plotted in Python.

runs.t: For the recent run of temperature shocks, the paper’s estimates imply that world income per person should grow by only about 0.5% a year from 2026 to 2031, leaving it about 5.9% below where baseline growth would put it in 2031 (Figure 4).

About 55% of the predicted shortfall stems from the coming El Niño, 37% from the 2023–25 warm years and about 7% from earlier years; the years after the El Niño barely change it (more on that below). Notably, even under the extreme view of Bilal and Känzig, the world continues to get richer over the next decade: by about 12% per person from 2025 to 2035, compared with about 19% if temperature shocks had no effect.

caption.t: World GDP per person under each view, indexed to 2026. Blue: the no-effect baseline, the IMF’s projection less its average past miss. Orange: the paper’s estimates applied to the temperature shocks since 2015 and to simulated temperatures after 2027. Dashed: the central contract’s cutoff. Shading shows 80% ranges, which include the paper’s statistical uncertainty and normal year-to-year swings in world growth. Data from the World Bank, the IMF and NOAA, plotted in Python.

runs.t: The prediction also depends on the years after the El Niño, because under the paper’s estimates every later global temperature shock moves GDP too. Strong El Niños are usually followed by cooler years, often La Niña years (Figure 5, left). So rather than ignore 2028–2031, I simulate them, drawing on what followed each of the seven strong El Niños since 1950. Measured against the authors’ trend, which was fitted before the 2023–24 jump, even a typical post-El Niño year still sits a little above it, so under the paper’s estimates those later years barely change the prediction by 2031 (Figure 5, right). The cutoffs account for this in advance; they will not be adjusted once the actual 2028–2031 temperatures are known.

caption.t: Left: global temperature shocks in the El Niño year and the three years after it, for the seven strong El Niños since 1950 (gray), their average (blue), and the 2027 estimate with the simulated years after it (orange). Right: the paper’s predicted effect on world GDP per person, with and without those simulated later years. The simulated years sit above the historical average because they are measured against the authors’ trend, fitted before the 2023–24 jump. Data from NOAA, plotted in Python.

blocks.text: Why 2031? The end year that best separates the two views

runs.t: Looking at Figure 2, it is tempting to measure growth over eight years or more, out to the bottom of the paper’s response. However, using a statistic known as Youden’s J, you can surmise the choice of end year that allows for optimal distinction between a world where the paper is correct and a world where the paper is incorrect - that is, it maximizes the chance of a “No” if the paper is correct plus the chance of a “Yes” if temperature shocks have no effect. The end year that maximized J was 2031.

Because the end year was chosen to maximize divergence between the two views, it deserves a brief explanation. The choice uses only information available before the contracts list: the paper’s published estimates, the IMF projection and its record of misses, and temperature forecasts. It uses no GDP data after 2025. Separation peaks around 2031 because two forces pull in opposite directions (Figure 6). The longer the period, the more of the paper’s predicted damage accumulates, and the shortfall keeps growing through 2031. But uncertainty about background growth also grows with every added year, and after 2031 the 2023–24 shocks start to wear off in the paper’s estimates. 2031 narrowly beats 2030 (J of 0.68 versus 0.67), and the end year will be fixed when the contracts list.

caption.t: How often the contract would resolve in line with the true view, depending on the last year of the growth period. Orange: the chance of a “No” if the paper is right. Blue: the chance of a “Yes” if temperature shocks have no effect. Black: their average, which is highest for 2031. Each end year uses its own best cutoff. Plotted in Python.

runs.t: The right cutoff also depends on how warm 2027 turns out, since a warmer 2027 means a bigger predicted shortfall. But NOAA will not publish its 2027 value until January 2028. Rather than wait, I propose three conditional contracts, one for each range of NOAA’s 2027 temperature, listed as soon as NOAA publishes its 2026 value in mid-January 2027:

rows.t: Will world GDP per person grow by more than
Chance of “Yes” if temperature shocks have no effect
Chance of “Yes” if the paper is right

runs.t: Each range is about equally likely today: the ranges are split halfway between the 20th, 50th and 80th percentiles of the current forecast for 2027 (1.41, 1.49 and 1.58 °C). When NOAA publishes the 2027 value, positions in the matching contract convert into a regular contract at the same cost, and the other two are refunded, which is how ForecastEx’s conditional contracts already work. A warmer 2027 means a lower cutoff, because the paper then predicts a bigger shortfall.

Within each range, the cutoff is set to make an incorrect resolution as unlikely as possible under either view. Based on current numbers, for the central contract, if the paper is right, there is an 82% chance that growth comes in at or below 1.1% a year, and if temperature shocks have no effect, there is an 87% chance that it comes in above it (Figure 7). In other words, whichever view is correct, the contract should resolve in line with it more than four out of five times.

caption.t: Simulated average growth from 2026 to 2031 under each view if NOAA’s 2027 temperature falls in the central range (1.46–1.53 °C), from 50,000 simulations that draw on the paper’s statistical uncertainty, the IMF baseline and its record of misses, and simulated temperatures after 2027. Plotted in Python.

runs.t: This design also makes the contract’s price unusually informative. If the paper were known to be right, a “Yes” contract should trade near 18 cents; if temperature shocks were known to have no effect, it should trade near 87 cents. Where the price actually sits between those values provides a running, public measure of how much credence informed participants give to one of the most consequential numbers in climate economics and even contemporary global policy.

blocks.text: When the contracts list and resolve

runs.t: The 2026 and 2027 temperatures are not yet final. The terms, including the end year, the three ranges and their cutoffs, will be fixed when NOAA publishes its 2026 annual temperature in mid-January 2027, and the
conditional contracts
will list right after.

Because growth is measured from the 2026 level, none of the outcomes are known when the contracts list. The contracts would resolve on October 1, 2032, about three months after the World Bank’s first estimate for 2031 (Figure 8).

caption.t: Timeline. The conditional contracts list after NOAA publishes its 2026 temperature, the matching one converts when NOAA publishes 2027’s, and all resolve on the World Bank’s 2031 figure as it stands on October 1, 2032. Plotted in Python.

runs.t: I assume that the IMF’s forecasts will keep running high, as they have; if the IMF has become unbiased, the central contract would resolve “No” only about half the time even if the paper is right.

The main objection on the skeptics' side would probably be that a global recession unrelated to temperature could coincide with El Niño and push the outcome to “No.” There is no clean way to rule that out, because under the paper’s view, temperature shocks themselves cut investment and productivity. Instead, the spread of background growth includes past recessions, which is why the contract resolves “No” about 13% of the time even with no temperature effect at all.

Technically, the biggest judgment call is the no-effect baseline: had I simply extended the 2000–2019 growth trend, the cutoff would be about 1.7% a year rather than 1.1%. And of course, a single episode cannot confirm or refute the paper.

Little or no effect of temperature shocks (about 1.6% a year)
